caseStudy.role: Solo project: design, iOS app and content pipeline
caseStudy.problem:
My portfolio already lived at aexomir.me as a quiet, typographic static site, and I wanted the same portfolio as a native iPhone app. Three constraints shaped it: it had to feel like iOS rather than a website in a frame, it had to still look like aexomir.me, and the content could never drift between the two.

Adding a project should update the site and the app together, with no App Store release, and I should be able to steer the installed app (pause it, nudge people to update, turn features off) without shipping code.
caseStudy.approach:
Both surfaces read one file, content.json, edited through Pages CMS. Each save is a commit; GitHub Actions validates it, renders the site and publishes the same JSON at aexomir.me/content.json.

The app shows the copy bundled at build time, then its last good downloaded copy from disk, then a fresh download on launch and on pull to refresh, and it checks the shape of every download before using it. An "app" section in the same file drives a maintenance banner, a new-version notice and switches for three features.

The UI uses system components wherever iOS users have expectations: Expo Router native tabs, large-title stacks, UIKit context menus and a form sheet. Liquid Glass stays on the navigation layer, so content remains flat and readable.
caseStudy.decisions:
A static JSON file instead of a server. There's no database, hosting bill or API to secure, and every edit is a commit with history and undo. The cost is no per-user data and no push, so the app only sees changes on launch or refresh.

Lighter validation in the app than in the build. The site build rejects bad content outright; the app only refuses a file whose shape would crash a screen, and otherwise keeps its last good copy.

Remote config that fails safe. If the "app" section is missing, every feature is on and no banner shows, and the update notice only fires for a well-formed version strictly newer than the installed one.

Over-the-air updates tied to the app version, so an update can never reach a binary with different native code. Any native change means a new version and a new build.

Custom interaction only where it carries identity: a weight wave through the name, and an Apps/Research switch that only claims horizontal pans, so scrolling and pull to refresh still work.
caseStudy.results:
The app runs the same content as aexomir.me from one CMS, and a content edit reaches it without a new build. It stays usable offline, with the last good copy or, on a first launch with no network, the bundled one, and pull to refresh reports whether anything changed. The maintenance banner, update notice and feature switches are all editable in Pages CMS.

The release path is wired too: buttons in the CMS run workflows that publish an over-the-air update or build for TestFlight through EAS. It runs on Expo SDK 58, React Native 0.88 and the React Compiler, iPhone only for now.
caseStudy.retrospective:
Get it onto TestFlight sooner. I built the release pipeline before having the Apple developer account to run it, so the one path a visitor actually needs, installing the app, is the one that's missing.

Persist small preferences from day one. The theme choice still resets on every launch, a small thing people notice straight away.

projects.name: Chrona
projects.summary: Automatic time tracking for Mac and iPhone, with on-device model inference and cross-device activity sync. In TestFlight.

caseStudy.role: Solo project: product, iOS app, macOS helper and release tooling
caseStudy.problem:
Manual time trackers depend on me remembering to press start, and I don't. I get pulled into something, work for two hours, and the timer was never running. Automatic trackers fix that by watching window titles, which means document names, the sites I visit and the names of private repos, and the commercial ones sync that to a server.

I wanted automatic tracking where none of that leaves hardware I own: no account, no backend, no analytics.
caseStudy.approach:
Chrona is two apps. The iPhone app (Expo, React Native, TypeScript) holds sessions, projects and rules. A Swift menu bar helper on the Mac watches the frontmost app and the focused window title, streams every change to the phone over the local network, and appends it to a seven-day activity ledger on disk. The phone finds the Mac over Bonjour (_chrona._tcp) through a local Expo module I wrote around Network.framework, and the helper sends nothing until the phone presents a six-character pairing code, compared in constant time.

Auto-tracking runs on rules I write: an app name plus optional window-title keywords, mapped to a project. When a rule matches, a timer starts. When I switch away for more than 15 seconds, it stops, and two minutes without input on the Mac puts the session on hold. When I stop a timer, the phone asks the Mac's ledger what happened in that window and shows a per-app breakdown, which I can trim before saving.
caseStudy.decisions:
Local-first over sync. Sessions, projects and rules live in MMKV encrypted with AES-256, with the key in the iOS Keychain. The phone and the Mac talk directly and nothing else. The cost is real: two phones mean two separate sets of data.

Two channels on one connection. The live stream drives the UI and is lossy by design. Per-app durations come from a request-response query against the Mac's ledger instead, so they stay correct when the phone was in my pocket or the Mac was asleep. If the Mac is unreachable when I save, the query is queued and retried for up to seven days.

Show what the app doesn't know. Every ledger answer includes coverage (observed, idle, locked, asleep, offline, unknown) that sums to the window length, so the app never implies it saw the whole session when it didn't.

An unsandboxed helper. Reading another app's window title needs the Accessibility API, which doesn't work inside the App Sandbox. That's a broad permission to ask for, and it's why the pairing gate matters: without it, any device on the network could read my window titles.

Predictable rules, no model. The matcher is a pure function: exact app name, every keyword present in the title, more keywords win. An app I use for ten minutes with no rule shows a quiet hint instead of being tracked behind my back. Search is keyword matching over my own sessions too: synchronous, local, no network call.
caseStudy.results: Version 1.1.0 shipped the Mac helper, pairing, wire protocol v2 with the usage query, per-app breakdowns, the backfill queue, auto-tracking rules, calendar mapping, home screen widgets and a Live Activity. Jest suites cover the stats, timer, auto-track matcher and calendar logic, Maestro flows cover starting and stopping a session and the Mac helper status, and CI runs typecheck, lint and tests on every pull request.
caseStudy.retrospective:
Sign and notarize the Mac helper from the start. Right now it's unsigned, so anyone else has to get past Gatekeeper before they can try the best part of the app.

Test Android early or drop it explicitly. The code paths exist but nothing on Android has been exercised, which is worse than a clear "iOS only".

projects.name: Semantic Correspondence with ViTs
projects.summary: Frozen vs fine-tuned DINOv2, DINOv3 and SAM backbones on SPair-71k. 76.4% PCK@0.1 with DINOv3, up from 53.6% frozen.

caseStudy.role: Course project, MSc AI at Politecnico di Torino · team of three. My part: the fine-tuning runs and the soft-argmax decoder (stages 2 and 3)
caseStudy.problem: Semantic correspondence means finding the same point on two different objects, like the left eye of one cat on another cat. We wanted to know how much of that pretrained vision backbones already encode, and how much a light fine-tune adds on top. We compared DINOv2 ViT-L/14, DINOv3 ViT-B/16 and the SAM ViT-B image encoder on SPair-71k: 12,234 test pairs and 88,328 keypoints.
caseStudy.approach:
The matcher is deliberately simple. Extract a dense patch feature map from each image, L2-normalize it, read the descriptor at the source keypoint, and pick the most similar target patch by cosine similarity. Scoring is PCK: a prediction counts if it lands within 0.05, 0.1, 0.15 or 0.2 of the target's bounding-box size.

The pipeline runs in four stages: frozen baselines; fine-tuning the last 1, 2 or 4 transformer blocks with an InfoNCE correspondence loss; a window soft-argmax decoder tuned on validation; and zero-shot transfer to PF-Pascal and PF-Willow. It's one Colab notebook, with features cached as float16 and checkpoints on Google Drive so runs resume across sessions.
caseStudy.decisions:
Change one thing at a time. The matcher stays fixed; only the backbone weights (stage 2) and the decoder (stage 3) change, so each gain can be attributed to one of them.

Train little. Only the last N blocks are unfrozen, trained with AdamW at a learning rate of 5e-6 for 3 epochs, batch size 1 with gradient accumulation of 4, and mixed precision. That's 9 runs: three backbones times three values of N.

Keep the test split clean. Checkpoints are chosen by validation PCK@0.1, and the soft-argmax sweep (temperatures 0.001 to 0.05, windows 3 to 11) also runs on validation. The test split is only evaluated after training.

Get below the patch grid. Argmax snaps to a 14- or 16-pixel patch. Window soft-argmax takes a temperature-weighted average in a small window around the peak, which gives sub-patch precision without touching the weights.
caseStudy.results:
Frozen, DINOv2 led with 55.5% PCK@0.1, DINOv3 scored 53.6% and SAM 24.4%. Fine-tuning lifted them to 72.9% (DINOv2, last 4 blocks), 74.5% (DINOv3, last 2) and 44.1% (SAM, last 2). More unfrozen blocks wasn't always better: DINOv3 fell to 66.4% with 4. Soft-argmax added another 0.6 to 1.9 points, taking DINOv3 to 76.4%, DINOv2 to 73.5% and SAM to 46.0%.

On PF-Willow, SPair fine-tuning helped all three backbones; DINOv3 went from 85.7% frozen to 89.2%. On PF-Pascal it helped DINOv2 (80.7% to 84.3%) and SAM (38.9% to 49.8%), but frozen DINOv3 was already at 86.5% and the fine-tuned version didn't beat it (86.0%). Both PF benchmarks normalize by image size rather than bounding box, so their numbers aren't directly comparable to SPair's.
caseStudy.retrospective:
Commit figures and qualitative match examples alongside the CSVs. The results only exist as tables today, so the work is hard to judge without re-running a GPU notebook.

Investigate surprises instead of just reporting them. DINOv3 dropping from 74.5% to 66.4% when unfreezing 4 blocks instead of 2 is the most interesting result here, and it deserved a proper look at learning rate and overfitting.

images.alt: Grouped bar chart of PCK@0.1 on SPair-71k. DINOv3 ViT-B/16: 53.6 frozen, 74.5 fine-tuned, 76.4 with soft-argmax. DINOv2 ViT-L/14: 55.5, 72.9, 73.5. SAM ViT-B: 24.4, 44.1, 46.0.
images.caption: Fine-tuning the last blocks adds about 20 points of PCK@0.1 for every backbone; soft-argmax adds up to 2 more, putting DINOv3 on top at 76.4.

projects.name: Heart Disease Risk Prediction
projects.summary: Logistic Regression, XGBoost and MLP with cross-site external validation, calibration and SHAP. ROC-AUC 0.949 on Cleveland.

caseStudy.role: Course project, MSc AI at Politecnico di Torino · team of two, with the work split evenly across every phase
caseStudy.problem: The UCI Heart Disease data comes from separate hospital cohorts. We trained on Cleveland and asked a harder question than held-out accuracy: how does the model hold up on patients from Hungary and Switzerland that it never saw in development, and how far can its probabilities be trusted? It's a research project, not a clinical tool.
caseStudy.approach:
We turned the label into any disease versus none and split Cleveland 70/15/15 with stratification: 212 train, 45 validation and 46 test rows. Hungarian (294 rows) and Swiss (123 rows) were held out as external test sets.

Three models share one preprocessing pipeline: logistic regression, XGBoost tuned with 50 Optuna trials, and a small MLP. A feature-engineering step expands the 13 raw predictors to 19 with interaction terms, then median imputation and scaling. Tuning and 5-fold cross-validation used Cleveland train only, the final models were fit on train plus validation, and the three test sets stayed untouched until final evaluation. Beyond ROC-AUC we reported average precision, F1, sensitivity and specificity, ran DeLong tests between the top two models on each split, tried Platt and isotonic calibration, ran a CORAL domain-adaptation ablation, and used SHAP to explain XGBoost.
caseStudy.decisions:
Measure the shift before modelling. Chi-square tests for categorical features and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests for continuous ones showed what we were up against. Hungarian is missing ca in 291 of 294 rows and thal in 266. Switzerland is 93.5% positive, with only 8 negatives in 123 rows.

Select on validation, not test. Cleveland validation ROC-AUC picked logistic regression as the best model. Threshold metrics use a fixed 0.5 cutoff rather than a clinically chosen operating point, and we list that as a limitation.

Don't over-read small numbers. With a 46-row test set and 8 Swiss negatives, we ran DeLong tests before calling any model better, and we read Switzerland's high average precision against its 93.5% base rate.

Keep adaptation honest. CORAL was evaluated only as an ablation and never used to select or train the models.
caseStudy.results:
On the held-out Cleveland test, logistic regression reached ROC-AUC 0.949, against 0.935 for both XGBoost and the MLP. On the external sites XGBoost was best, at 0.876 on Hungarian and 0.720 on Switzerland. The only significant DeLong difference was XGBoost over logistic regression on Switzerland (0.065, p = 0.031), and with 8 negatives that is weak evidence.

Calibration helped in places: isotonic calibration cut logistic regression's expected calibration error on the Cleveland test from 0.106 to 0.072. It stayed poor on Switzerland, where XGBoost only improved from 0.452 to 0.394. CORAL didn't help: for XGBoost on Switzerland it lowered ROC-AUC from 0.720 to 0.628 and sensitivity from 0.470 to 0.261. SHAP ranked ca, the engineered cp × thal interaction and cp as the top three features.

The takeaway: strong internal discrimination did not carry over evenly to other sites.
caseStudy.retrospective:
Make the evaluation reproducible end to end. The final notebook imports a module that is no longer in the repo, and two committed figures drifted from the final result tables. Every table and figure should come from one script, in one run.

Pick a clinical operating point. A fixed 0.5 threshold is easy to compare but says little about how the model would actually be used.

images.alt: SHAP beeswarm summary for the XGBoost model. The top-ranked features are ca, cp_x_thal, cp, age_x_oldpeak, thal and sex; high values of ca and cp_x_thal push predictions toward disease.
images.caption: SHAP summary for XGBoost: vessel count (ca) and the engineered chest-pain × thalassemia interaction drive predictions most.
